title: Halal, Haram and the Penalties
question: Is the list of what Allah forbids long or short?
intro: Halal means permitted; haram means forbidden. The Quran's starting point is generous: eat of what is lawful and good (2:168). It names what is forbidden, and it condemns people who invent prohibitions and attribute them to Allah (16:116). Scholars draw a principle from this: things are lawful unless shown otherwise.

It also names a few grave wrongs with fixed penalties in this world: unlawful sex, falsely accusing someone of it, theft, armed robbery, and murder. These verses are often quoted without their conditions. Today you will read them with those conditions: strict proof, a court rather than individuals, and the door of repentance the verses themselves keep open.
Where details come from hadith and the schools of law rather than the verse, the label says so.

passages.context: Makkah. 6:151-153 gives a longer list, and 4:31 promises that avoiding the major sins wipes away lesser ones.
passages.point: The forbidden is named: indecency open or hidden, sin, oppression, associating partners with Allah, and speaking about Allah without knowledge.
passages.label: stated

passages.context: Madinah. 5:3 adds animals killed by strangling, blows or falls; 5:5 allows the food of the People of the Book.
passages.point: Only a few foods are forbidden: carrion, blood, pork, and what is dedicated to other than Allah. Under real necessity, there is no sin.
passages.label: stated

passages.context: The last of three stages on alcohol, after 2:219 and 4:43.
passages.point: Intoxicants and gambling are called defilement from Satan that breeds enmity and keeps people from prayer. Scholars read "avoid it" as a complete ban.
passages.label: stated

passages.context: Proof requires four witnesses to the act (24:4, 24:13) or a free confession.
passages.point: Proven unlawful sex (zina) carries a hundred lashes, applied by a court without pity suspending the law.
passages.label: differ
passages.note: Sahih's "[unmarried]" follows the majority, who apply stoning to married offenders from hadith in al-Bukhari and Muslim. A minority, early and modern, hold that 24:2 covers all.

passages.context: Madinah. The penalty is stated; its conditions come from the Sunnah and the jurists.
passages.point: Applied only with firm proof, above a minimum value, from a secured place, and not under need or doubt; 'Umar suspended it in a famine. 5:39 opens repentance.
passages.label: explained

passages.from: O you who have believed, prescribed for you
passages.context: Reports say it ended tribal feuds where the strong took many lives for one. 2:179: in retribution there is life.
passages.point: Murder is answered by equal retribution through the law, yet the victim's family may forgive and accept compensation (diyah), which the verse calls a mercy.
passages.label: stated

visual.title: Lines not to cross
visual.caption: The commands of 6:151-153, in the order the verses give them. Ibn Mas'ud is reported to have called these verses the Prophet's ﷺ sealed testament.
visual.label: stated

items.label: Children
items.text: Do not kill them for fear of poverty.

items.label: Indecency
items.text: Do not even approach it, open or hidden.

items.label: Life
items.text: Take no life except by legal right.

items.label: Orphans' wealth
items.text: Guard it in the best way until they mature.

items.label: Measure
items.text: Give full measure and weight in justice.

items.label: Words
items.text: Be just when you speak, even about a relative.

items.label: The straight path
items.text: Follow it; other ways scatter you from His way.

word.nuance: Something set apart and fenced off. The same root names the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram) and the sacred months: what is haram is protected, either because it is holy or because it harms. Its opposite, halal, comes from a root meaning to untie: released for use.

mixup.myth: Islamic law is mostly a list of harsh punishments that any Muslim may carry out.
mixup.truth: Only a few fixed penalties appear in the Quran, each bound by strict proof, such as four witnesses (24:4). Classical scholars agreed they belong to a lawful court, never to individuals, and that doubt prevents them. The verses also keep repentance open (5:34, 5:39, 24:5). Most of Islamic law concerns worship, family, trade and character.

remember: The default is lawful and good; the forbidden is named, and inventing prohibitions is itself condemned (2:168, 7:33, 16:116).
Fixed penalties are few, need strict proof, and belong to a court, never to individuals.
Avoiding major sins wipes away lesser ones, and repentance is offered within the penalty verses themselves (4:31, 5:39).

quiz.q: How many witnesses does the Quran require for an accusation of unlawful sex?
quiz.why: 24:4 punishes those who accuse and "then do not produce four witnesses"; 24:13 repeats the requirement.

quiz.q: What does 2:173 say about someone forced by necessity to eat forbidden food?
options: There is no sin upon them
They must refuse even if starving
quiz.why: 2:173: "whoever is forced [by necessity], neither desiring [it] nor transgressing [its limit], there is no sin upon him."

quiz.q: In 2:178, what may a murder victim's family choose instead of retribution?
options: Exile of the killer's whole tribe
quiz.why: 2:178: "whoever overlooks from his brother anything, then there should be a suitable follow-up and payment to him with good conduct. This is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy."

reflect: Which of the lines in 6:151-153 do you most want to guard more carefully in your own life?
